<SYSTEM>This is the full developer documentation for Chirograph</SYSTEM>

# Chirograph

> Typed HTTP clients generated from OpenAPI documents at build time. One MSBuild item, a Kiota or Refitter client, registered with IHttpClientFactory.

A chirograph was a medieval contract written twice on one sheet and cut apart, so each half proved the other. Here the OpenAPI document and the generated client are the two halves: Chirograph keeps them together by generating the client from the document on every build that needs it.

Declare a client with one item. Where its document comes from is inferred from the `Include`:

* A file

  ```xml
  <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
    <Sdk Name="Chirograph" Version="1.0.0" />


    <ItemGroup>
      <OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" />
    </ItemGroup>
  </Project>
  ```

* A server project

  ```xml
  <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
    <Sdk Name="Chirograph" Version="1.0.0" />


    <ItemGroup>
      <OpenApiClient Include="../Rockets.Api/Rockets.Api.csproj" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" />
    </ItemGroup>
  </Project>
  ```

* A URL

  ```xml
  <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
    <Sdk Name="Chirograph" Version="1.0.0" />


    <ItemGroup>
      <OpenApiClient
        Include="https://rockets.example.com/openapi/v1.json"
        Generator="Refitter"
        ClientName="RocketsClient"
        DocumentCache="openapi/rockets.json"
      />
    </ItemGroup>
  </Project>
  ```

Then register it, and give it a base address in `Clients:RocketsClient:BaseAddress`:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient();
```

Note

Chirograph has no release on nuget.org yet. [Getting started](guides/) shows how to pack it from a clone until the first beta ships.

Two generators you already use

Kiota, or Refit through Refitter. Chirograph generates no code of its own, so it keeps each generator’s fidelity and follows their releases by changing a version.

Three sources

A file in the project, a server project in the same build, or a URL with a document cache you can commit.

Quiet builds

Tools come from the packages folder, output stays in `obj`, generation is incremental, and the generators’ telemetry is off.

Registered

Every client gets an `Add<ClientName>()` extension that registers it with `IHttpClientFactory` and returns the `IHttpClientBuilder`.

[Getting started](guides/)Add the SDK, declare a client and call it.

[Concepts](concepts/)Sources, generators, registration, the document cache and how generation runs.

[Reference](reference/)Every metadata value, property and diagnostic code.

[Compared with](concepts/compared-with/)OpenApiReference, Refitter.MSBuild, hand-written targets and source generators.

# Concepts

> Sources, generators, registration, the document cache and how generation runs.

A **client** is one `OpenApiClient` item and everything generated for it. It has one **document**, an OpenAPI description, which comes from a **source**: a file, a server project or a URL. A **generator**, Kiota or Refitter, turns the document into code, and a **registration**, `Add<ClientName>()`, puts the client into `IHttpClientFactory` with its **base address** read from configuration.

* [Sources](sources/): how the kind of source is inferred from `Include`.
* [Generators](generators/): Kiota and Refitter, what each writes, and the packages each adds.
* [Registration](registration/): the extension method, the configuration key and chaining on `IHttpClientBuilder`.
* [Document cache](document-cache/): what happens to a URL’s document between builds.
* [How generation runs](how-generation-runs/): tools, `obj`, incrementality, design-time builds and telemetry.
* [Compared with](compared-with/): where Chirograph sits among the other ways to get a client.

The [glossary](https://github.com/RocketSurgeonsGuild/Chirograph/blob/main/GLOSSARY.md) defines each of these words once.

# Compared with

> Where Chirograph sits among OpenApiReference, Kiota and Refitter's own build integrations, hand-written targets, and generators that ship their own code generation.

Chirograph is the MSBuild layer for the two generators .NET teams already choose: Kiota, and [Refit](https://github.com/reactiveui/refit) through Refitter. It generates no code of its own, so it inherits each generator’s fidelity and keeps up with their releases by changing a version. What it adds:

* one item per client;
* three sources, including a sibling server project and a URL with a committable cache;
* incremental, offline-capable, telemetry-free builds;
* an `IHttpClientFactory` registration, and with it a Dovetail joint ([with Dovetail](../../guides/with-dovetail/)).

## `OpenApiReference` and `dotnet openapi`

[Section titled “OpenApiReference and dotnet openapi”](#openapireference-and-dotnet-openapi)

`Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Client` is deprecated as of .NET 10 ([breaking change](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/compatibility/aspnet-core/10/apidescription-client-deprecated), [dotnet/aspnetcore#59208](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/59208)). Microsoft now points at each generator’s own tooling, and at committing the generated code or running generation in a custom pre-build step. Chirograph is that pre-build step, written once. [Migrating from OpenApiReference](../../guides/migrating-from-openapireference/) maps one item onto the other.

## Kiota with a hand-written target

[Section titled “Kiota with a hand-written target”](#kiota-with-a-hand-written-target)

Kiota dropped its own MSBuild integration for lack of use, and points people at an `Exec` task ([microsoft/kiota#3005](https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/issues/3005)). Blog posts show that target for one server project and one tool manifest ([Meziantou](https://www.meziantou.net/generate-a-kiota-client-at-build-time-from-an-asp-net-core-openapi-file.htm)). Chirograph is that target for any number of clients and all three sources, with the incrementality, design-time behaviour and telemetry settings already worked out, and without a tool manifest.

## Refitter.MSBuild

[Section titled “Refitter.MSBuild”](#refittermsbuild)

[Refitter.MSBuild](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Refitter.MSBuild) runs Refitter from the build. It finds `.refitter` files by scanning the project folder, and runs on every build: its target has no inputs or outputs and no design-time guard. It writes into the project folder by default, has telemetry on by default, and is Refit-only.

Chirograph drives the Refitter CLI instead. It writes the `.refitter` file into `obj` itself, from the item, so each Refitter client gets the same incrementality and design-time rules as a Kiota client.

## Generators with their own code generation

[Section titled “Generators with their own code generation”](#generators-with-their-own-code-generation)

[AutoSDK](https://github.com/tryAGI/AutoSDK) and [OpenApiWeaver](https://dev.to/polymind/openapiweaver-generate-type-safe-c-clients-from-openapi-at-compile-time-with-source-generators-5e79) also offer one item per client, but generate the client with their own code generators. AutoSDK is still before 1.0. OpenApiWeaver’s item, `OpenApiWeaverDocument`, is close to Chirograph’s.

Pick one of them if you want their client. Pick Chirograph if you want Kiota’s or Refit’s.

## Summary

[Section titled “Summary”](#summary)

|                     | Chirograph        | `OpenApiReference` | Hand-written `Exec` | Refitter.MSBuild   |
| ------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------ |
| Generators          | Kiota, Refitter   | NSwag by default   | Whatever you call   | Refitter           |
| Status              | Active            | Deprecated         | Yours to maintain   | Active             |
| Declared with       | One item          | One item           | A target            | A `.refitter` file |
| Generated code goes | `obj`             | `obj`              | Your choice         | The project folder |
| Generates when      | Something changed | —                  | Your choice         | Every build        |
| Generator telemetry | Off               | —                  | Your choice         | On by default      |

# Document cache

> How a URL source keeps its last download, falls back to it when the URL can't be reached, and how committing it and UpdateDocumentCache decide when an API change reaches the client.

The document cache is the last document a [URL source](../sources/) downloaded. Only URL sources have one: a file is its own document, and a server project writes its document on every build.

## Where it lives

[Section titled “Where it lives”](#where-it-lives)

By default the cache is the client’s copy of the document in `obj`, `obj/<configuration>/<framework>/openapi/<ClientName>/openapi.json`. It survives builds, but not `dotnet clean` or a clean clone.

`DocumentCache` names a file in the project instead, relative to the project. That file can be committed, so every clone and every CI agent starts with a cache.

## What a build does

[Section titled “What a build does”](#what-a-build-does)

For each URL client, a build:

1. Decides whether to download. It downloads unless updating is off (below) and the cache exists.
2. Downloads the document into the client’s `download/` folder, retrying twice.
3. If the download succeeded and differs from the cache, **updates** the cache: overwrites it with the download.
4. If the download failed, uses the cache, with warning [`CHIRO104`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro104). With no cache, the build fails with [`CHIRO105`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro105).
5. Generates the client from the cache, through the same copy-when-changed step as every source.

So a download that returns what the cache already holds changes no file and regenerates nothing.

## Updating

[Section titled “Updating”](#updating)

Updating is on by default: every build that reaches the URL takes the API’s latest document. That suits a cache in `obj`, or a committed cache whose diffs you review.

Turn it off to decide when a change reaches the client. With updating off and a cache present, the build doesn’t download at all:

* for every client, with the property `ChirographUpdateOpenApiDocumentCache` set to `false`;
* for one client, with the metadata `UpdateDocumentCache="false"`, which wins over the property.

To take the changes later, build once with `-p:ChirographUpdateOpenApiDocumentCache=true` (which works for clients that don’t set the metadata), or delete the cache file. A client with updating off and no cache still downloads once, to fill it.

[From a URL](../../guides/from-a-url/) walks through committing the cache and building in CI without network.

# Generators

> Kiota and Refitter compared, what each writes, the command line Chirograph runs, and the packages it adds to the project for each.

A generator is the tool that turns a document into client code. Chirograph runs one of two, chosen per client with `Generator`. Neither is a Roslyn source generator: each is a .NET tool that runs as a process during the build. See [How generation runs](../how-generation-runs/).

|                        | Kiota                                                            | Refitter                                                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What it writes         | A client class, `<ClientName>`, with request builders and models | A [Refit](https://github.com/reactiveui/refit) interface, `I<ClientName>`, and its contracts |
| A call looks like      | `await client.Rockets[id].GetAsync()`                            | `await client.GetRocket(id)`                                                                 |
| Package added          | `Microsoft.Kiota.Bundle`, and `Microsoft.Extensions.Http`        | `Refit.HttpClientFactory`                                                                    |
| Without a base address | Uses the first server of the document                            | Needs one                                                                                    |
| Tool package           | `Microsoft.OpenApi.Kiota`                                        | `Refitter`                                                                                   |

Choose Kiota for a large API, or one whose shape changes often: its request builders follow the paths. Choose Refitter for a smaller API where one method per operation reads better, or when you already use Refit.

## The packages added to the project

[Section titled “The packages added to the project”](#the-packages-added-to-the-project)

The generated code needs a runtime library, which Chirograph adds as an implicit `PackageReference` when at least one client uses the generator:

* **Kiota**: `Microsoft.Kiota.Bundle`, and `Microsoft.Extensions.Http` for the registration. A project that also has a Refitter client doesn’t get `Microsoft.Extensions.Http`: `Refit.HttpClientFactory` brings it, possibly at a newer version than the one Chirograph was packed with, and adding the older one would be a downgrade (NU1605).
* **Refitter**: `Refit.HttpClientFactory`, which brings Refit, its source generator and `Microsoft.Extensions.Http`.
* **`Authentication="Azure"`** on any client: `Azure.Identity`.
* **`Authentication="ClientCredentials"`** on any client: `Duende.AccessTokenManagement` 4.x, which brings `Microsoft.Extensions.Http` (so a Kiota client’s isn’t added) and `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` (so the registration’s [resilience](../registration/#resilience) block is written too, off unless `Resilience` is `true` or an object of its settings).

A package the project references itself wins: its own `PackageReference` and its version are left alone, and Chirograph adds nothing. So reference a package yourself to choose its version, or set the matching [property](../../reference/properties/).

Under [Central Package Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/nuget/consume-packages/central-package-management) (`ManagePackageVersionsCentrally`), a package that has a `PackageVersion` gets a plain `PackageReference`, without a version and not implicit, so the central version wins. A package without a `PackageVersion` keeps the implicit reference at Chirograph’s version, which NuGet allows. So pin a package in `Directory.Packages.props` to choose its version; the project doesn’t need to reference it.

## What Chirograph passes

[Section titled “What Chirograph passes”](#what-chirograph-passes)

Kiota runs as:

```sh
kiota generate --language CSharp --openapi <document> --class-name <ClientName> --namespace-name <Namespace> \
  --output <client folder>/generated --clean-output --exclude-backward-compatible --log-level Warning <Options>
```

Refitter runs with a settings file Chirograph writes, `<ClientName>.refitter`, which sets the document, the namespace, the interface name (`useOpenApiTitle` off) and cancellation tokens on every method:

```sh
refitter --settings-file <client folder>/<ClientName>.refitter --output <client folder>/generated/<ClientName>.cs \
  --no-logging --no-banner --simple-output <Options>
```

`Options` goes last, so you can add to what Chirograph passes. Don’t change the output, the class or interface name or the namespace there: the registration expects them.

## Versions

[Section titled “Versions”](#versions)

Each Chirograph release is packed with a version of each tool and of each package it adds. Set `ChirographKiotaVersion` or `ChirographRefitterVersion` to run another version of a tool; the [properties](../../reference/properties/) list them all. A different tool version generates every client of that generator again.

# How generation runs

> How Chirograph fetches the generators with PackageDownload, generates into obj, stays incremental, behaves in design-time builds and keeps telemetry off.

## The tools come from the packages folder

[Section titled “The tools come from the packages folder”](#the-tools-come-from-the-packages-folder)

Kiota and Refitter are .NET tools. Chirograph declares each one a client uses as a `PackageDownload`, so NuGet restores it with the project’s other packages, and the build runs it from the packages folder with `dotnet exec`. Nothing is installed globally or in a tool manifest, and once the packages are restored, a file or server-project source needs no network.

That is why Chirograph is an MSBuild SDK rather than an ordinary package: NuGet restore never sees a `PackageDownload` or `PackageReference` that a package’s own `build/` targets declare.

The tools run on .NET 10, rolling forward to a newer runtime when .NET 10 isn’t installed, so a build needs the .NET SDK 10.0.100 or later. A tool that isn’t in the packages folder fails the build with [`CHIRO106`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro106): restore the project.

## When it runs

[Section titled “When it runs”](#when-it-runs)

The target `ChirographGenerateOpenApiClients` runs after the project’s references are resolved, and before compilation. For a server project source, that means the server has been built. The target is the hook to run something after the clients are generated:

```xml
<Target Name="ListClients" AfterTargets="ChirographGenerateOpenApiClients">
  <Message Importance="high" Text="Generated: @(OpenApiClient->'%(ClientName)')" />
</Target>
```

To run something before, while a client’s document can still be written, hook `ChirographBeforeGenerateOpenApiClients`, which runs before any document is checked, read or downloaded:

```xml
<Target Name="ExportApiSpec" BeforeTargets="ChirographBeforeGenerateOpenApiClients">
  <Exec Command="dotnet run --project ../Exporter -- $(MSBuildProjectDirectory)/openapi.json" />
</Target>
```

Not `BeforeTargets="ChirographGenerateOpenApiClients"`: MSBuild runs that target’s dependencies, which generate the clients, before the targets hooked before it. Adding a target to `ChirographGenerateOpenApiClientsDependsOn` works as well. Neither hook runs in a design-time build.

A project without `OpenApiClient` items doesn’t run it, and gets no packages or downloads.

## Everything stays in `obj`

[Section titled “Everything stays in obj”](#everything-stays-in-obj)

Each client has a folder, `obj/<configuration>/<framework>/openapi/<ClientName>/` by default (`ChirographOpenApiClientsDirectory` moves the parent). The generated code and the registration are added to `Compile` there, and never written into the project. `dotnet clean` removes them. [Generated code](../../reference/generated-code/) lists the folder’s files.

## Incremental

[Section titled “Incremental”](#incremental)

A client is generated again only when something it depends on changed:

1. The document is copied into the client’s folder only when its content differs from the copy there.
2. The client’s settings (the generator, the tool’s version, `ClientName`, `Namespace` and `Options`) are written to `settings.txt` only when they differ.
3. The generator runs only when the copy or `settings.txt` is newer than the client’s last generation.

So a build with nothing changed runs no generator, and neither does a server that writes the same document again. A change to one client regenerates only that client.

## Design-time builds

[Section titled “Design-time builds”](#design-time-builds)

An IDE runs design-time builds to learn a project’s compile items. Those never run a generator: they only add the code an earlier build generated, so IntelliSense sees the client without the IDE downloading or generating anything. They check nothing either: a client with a mistake loads without an error and without creating a folder, and the next build reports it. After you change a client, build once to update it.

## No telemetry

[Section titled “No telemetry”](#no-telemetry)

A build is no place to call home. Chirograph runs the tools with:

* `KIOTA_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=true`, which turns Kiota’s telemetry off;
* `KIOTA_OFFLINE_ENABLED=true`, which turns Kiota’s update check off;
* `DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1`;
* Refitter’s `--no-logging`, which turns its telemetry off.

## Output and failures

[Section titled “Output and failures”](#output-and-failures)

What a tool writes is logged at low importance, and not parsed for warnings (Kiota warns about every document without a server). When a tool exits with an error, the build fails with [`CHIRO107`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro107), which includes what the tool wrote. Run the build with `-v:n` to see the tools’ output on success.

# Registration

> The Add<ClientName>() extension every client gets, its generated <ClientName>Options, filled from Clients:<ClientName> and a connection string and validated at startup, and configuring the client further on IHttpClientBuilder.

Every client gets a registration: a public extension method on `IServiceCollection`, written next to the generated code. For a client named `RocketsClient` it is:

```csharp
public static IHttpClientBuilder AddRocketsClient(this IServiceCollection services, Action<RocketsClientOptions>? configure = null);
```

It is in the client’s namespace, in a static class named `RocketsClientServiceCollectionExtensions`, next to the client’s options, `RocketsClientOptions`. Both are public, so an application can register and configure a client that a library it references generated. The project of the client writes no code of its own.

## What it registers

[Section titled “What it registers”](#what-it-registers)

* **Kiota:** a named `HttpClient`, `RocketsClient`, and the typed client `RocketsClient`, built on Kiota’s `HttpClientRequestAdapter` with the authentication provider from the container, unless the options configure an authentication (see [Authentication](#authentication)).
* **Refitter:** `IRocketsClient`, through Refit’s `AddRefitGeneratedClient`. Refit’s source generator writes the implementation at build time, so there is no reflection.
* **Both:** the options, `RocketsClientOptions`, with their validation, which runs when the host starts.

Resolve the client from the container, or inject it:

```csharp
public sealed class LaunchService(RocketsClient rockets) { … }    // Kiota
public sealed class LaunchService(IRocketsClient rockets) { … }   // Refitter
```

## The options

[Section titled “The options”](#the-options)

`RocketsClientOptions` holds what the registration applies to the client each time its `HttpClient` is created. Generated code fills it from configuration, without the reflection binder, so it is safe for trimming and AOT. The registration reads it through `IOptionsMonitor<RocketsClientOptions>`, so a configuration reload applies when the client’s handlers rotate.

The options are filled from three sources, from lowest to highest:

1. The keys under `Clients:RocketsClient`.
2. Code: the `configure` argument of `AddRocketsClient()`, and any `services.Configure<RocketsClientOptions>(…)`, wherever it is called, in the order they are registered: a `Configure` registered before `AddRocketsClient()` runs before the `configure` argument, one registered after runs after it.
3. The client’s [connection string](#the-connection-string), applied as a post-configuration, so it wins over everything else.

Code that must win over the connection string uses `services.PostConfigure<RocketsClientOptions>(…)`.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient(options => options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));
```

## Configuration

[Section titled “Configuration”](#configuration)

The section’s path is an internal constant on the registration class, `RocketsClientServiceCollectionExtensions.SectionKey`.

```json
{
    "Clients": {
        "RocketsClient": {
            "BaseAddress": "https://rockets.example.com/",
            "Timeout": "00:00:30",
            "DefaultRequestHeaders": {
                "X-Api-Version": "2"
            },
            "Resilience": true
        }
    }
}
```

| Key                     | Type                 | Effect                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ConnectionString`      | string               | The client’s [connection string](#the-connection-string).                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `BaseAddress`           | absolute URI         | `HttpClient.BaseAddress`, `http` or `https`. Alias `Endpoint`. Without one, Kiota uses the document’s first server, Refit fails when called, unless [service discovery](#service-discovery) is on.                                                      |
| `Timeout`               | `TimeSpan`           | `HttpClient.Timeout`, written as `hh:mm:ss` in the invariant culture (`00:00:00.5` is half a second). Without one, the `HttpClient` default of 100 seconds stays.                                                                                       |
| `DefaultRequestHeaders` | string to string map | Each entry is added to `HttpClient.DefaultRequestHeaders`, so every request sends it. Not in a connection string.                                                                                                                                       |
| `Resilience`            | bool or object       | `true` keeps the standard resilience handler (`AddStandardResilienceHandler()`): retries, timeouts and a circuit breaker; an object sets its [settings](#resilience). It is read only when the project references Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience. |
| `AllowedHosts`          | array of hosts       | More hosts than the `BaseAddress` host that may receive the client’s [credentials](#which-hosts-get-the-credentials). In a connection string, a comma-separated list.                                                                                   |
| `Authentication`        | method               | How the client authenticates: `None` (the default, the [container](#from-the-container) decides), `ApiKey`, `Bearer` or `Basic` ([configured](#configured-authentication)).                                                                             |
| `ApiKey`                | string               | The key of `ApiKey`. Alias `Key`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `ApiKeyHeader`          | string               | The header `ApiKey` sends the key in, `X-Api-Key` by default.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `ApiKeyQuery`           | string               | The query parameter `ApiKey` sends the key in, instead of a header.                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `Token`                 | string               | The token of `Bearer`. In code, `TokenProvider` can give it instead.                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `Username`              | string               | The user name of `Basic`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `Password`              | string               | The password of `Basic`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `CertificatePath`       | path                 | A [client certificate](#client-certificate-mtls), a PKCS#12 (`.pfx`, `.p12`) or PEM file.                                                                                                                                                               |
| `CertificatePassword`   | string               | The password of the PKCS#12 file, or of the encrypted PEM key.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `CertificateKeyPath`    | path                 | The PEM private key, when `CertificatePath` is a PEM certificate without its key.                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `CertificateThumbprint` | string               | A client certificate in a certificate store, instead of a file.                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `CertificateStore`      | `<location>/<name>`  | The store of `CertificateThumbprint`: `CurrentUser/My` (the default) or `LocalMachine/My`, say.                                                                                                                                                         |

Keys are case-insensitive. A key that isn’t set leaves the `HttpClient` as it is. Any configuration source works: the environment variable `Clients__RocketsClient__DefaultRequestHeaders__X-Api-Version` sets a header, for example.

### The connection string

[Section titled “The connection string”](#the-connection-string)

A client can take its settings as one SqlClient-style string, as a database does. It is read from `Clients:RocketsClient:ConnectionString` (`RocketsClientServiceCollectionExtensions.ConnectionStringKey`) when that key exists, else from `ConnectionStrings:RocketsClient`, which is where Aspire and most hosts put connection strings. The first one found is used, and the two are never merged.

```json
{
    "ConnectionStrings": {
        "RocketsClient": "Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;Timeout=00:00:30"
    }
}
```

It has the syntax of `DbConnectionStringBuilder`:

* `key=value` pairs separated by `;`. Whitespace around keys and unquoted values is trimmed.
* A value that contains `;`, or leading or trailing spaces, is quoted with `'` or `"`. A doubled quote stands for itself: `Endpoint='https://rockets.example.com/?a=1;b=2'`.
* An unquoted value may contain `=`.

It takes the keys of the table above, except `ConnectionString` and `DefaultRequestHeaders`, and the [resilience settings](#resilience), as `MaxRetryAttempts`, `AttemptTimeout` and the like. The parser is stricter than `DbConnectionStringBuilder`: an unknown key and a key given twice (an alias with its key, `Endpoint` and `BaseAddress`, too) are errors.

When an application already has a connection string named after the client for something else, a database say, set `Clients:RocketsClient:ConnectionString` to an empty value. The client then reads no connection string:

```json
{
    "ConnectionStrings": { "RocketsClient": "Data Source=db;Initial Catalog=rockets" },
    "Clients": { "RocketsClient": { "ConnectionString": "", "BaseAddress": "https://rockets.example.com/" } }
}
```

## Validation

[Section titled “Validation”](#validation)

The registration validates the options with a generated `IValidateOptions<RocketsClientOptions>`, and asks for it at startup (`ValidateOnStart`). Under a host, a bad client stops the host from starting, with an `OptionsValidationException` that lists every problem. With a bare `ServiceCollection`, the same exception is thrown when the client is first created.

It fails on:

* an unknown key in the connection string, or a key given twice there (an alias with its key too);
* a value that doesn’t parse (`Timeout`, `Resilience` and its [settings](#resilience), `Authentication`), or a malformed connection string;
* a `BaseAddress` that isn’t an absolute `http` or `https` URI (or, with [service discovery](#service-discovery), a service-discovery address), or a `Timeout` that isn’t positive;
* with service discovery, no service-discovery provider registered by the application;
* an `Authentication` without the keys it needs (the keys of another method are ignored), or with no host to send the credentials to (neither `BaseAddress` nor `AllowedHosts`);
* a [client certificate](#client-certificate-mtls) given by both a path and a thumbprint, a `CertificatePassword` or `CertificateKeyPath` without a `CertificatePath`, a `CertificateStore` without a `CertificateThumbprint`, a file that doesn’t exist, and a certificate that doesn’t load with its private key (a wrong password, say).

Under `Clients:RocketsClient` the keys are lenient, as configuration binding is: a key the client doesn’t read is ignored, of a key and its alias (`Endpoint` and `BaseAddress`) the later one wins, and a key that must be a value but holds an object is ignored with a warning, logged when the application registers an `ILoggerFactory`.

The messages name the source (`Clients:RocketsClient:Timeout`, `ConnectionStrings:RocketsClient`) and the key, never a value, so they are safe to log even when a value is a secret. In a connection string, an unknown key is named only when it reads as one (letters, digits and spaces, not followed by another `=`): an unquoted secret holding a `;`, `Key=ab;cd==` say, is reported as an unrecognised part, without its text.

## Resilience

[Section titled “Resilience”](#resilience)

Chirograph adds no resilience package. When the project references [Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience) (directly or through another package or project), the build sees it among the resolved references and writes the resilience code into the registration: it calls `AddStandardResilienceHandler()` on the client’s builder, and takes the handler out again when the client’s handlers are built unless `Resilience` is `true`. Without the package the registration has no such code, it compiles, and `Resilience` is ignored.

`Resilience` is either `true` or `false`, or an object of the handler’s settings, named as `HttpStandardResilienceOptions` names them (the [standard resilience handler](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/resilience/http-resilience#standard-resilience-handler-defaults)). An object keeps the handler, unless its `Enabled` is `false`, and a setting it leaves out keeps the handler’s default:

```json
{
    "Clients": {
        "RocketsClient": {
            "Resilience": {
                "Retry": { "MaxRetryAttempts": 5, "BackoffType": "Exponential", "Delay": "00:00:01" },
                "AttemptTimeout": { "Timeout": "00:00:05" },
                "TotalRequestTimeout": { "Timeout": "00:01:00" },
                "CircuitBreaker": { "FailureRatio": 0.2, "SamplingDuration": "00:00:30" }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

| Setting                                                      | Type                                | Default       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `Enabled`                                                    | bool                                | `true`        |
| `RateLimiter:DefaultRateLimiterOptions:PermitLimit`          | int                                 | `1000`        |
| `RateLimiter:DefaultRateLimiterOptions:QueueLimit`           | int                                 | `0`           |
| `RateLimiter:DefaultRateLimiterOptions:QueueProcessingOrder` | `OldestFirst`, `NewestFirst`        | `OldestFirst` |
| `TotalRequestTimeout:Timeout`                                | `TimeSpan`                          | `00:00:30`    |
| `Retry:MaxRetryAttempts`                                     | int                                 | `3`           |
| `Retry:BackoffType`                                          | `Constant`, `Linear`, `Exponential` | `Exponential` |
| `Retry:UseJitter`                                            | bool                                | `true`        |
| `Retry:Delay`                                                | `TimeSpan`                          | `00:00:02`    |
| `Retry:MaxDelay`                                             | `TimeSpan`                          | none          |
| `Retry:ShouldRetryAfterHeader`                               | bool                                | `true`        |
| `CircuitBreaker:FailureRatio`                                | number, 0 to 1                      | `0.1`         |
| `CircuitBreaker:MinimumThroughput`                           | int                                 | `100`         |
| `CircuitBreaker:SamplingDuration`                            | `TimeSpan`                          | `00:00:30`    |
| `CircuitBreaker:BreakDuration`                               | `TimeSpan`                          | `00:00:05`    |
| `AttemptTimeout:Timeout`                                     | `TimeSpan`                          | `00:00:10`    |

The registration reads them without reflection into `RocketsClientOptions.ResilienceOptions`, so code can change them too (`AddRocketsClient(o => o.ResilienceOptions.Retry.MaxRetryAttempts = 5)`), and hands them to the handler whenever the options are filled, when configuration reloads too. A value that doesn’t parse fails [validation](#validation); Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience checks the rest when the host starts (`MaxRetryAttempts` at least 1, an `AttemptTimeout` shorter than the `TotalRequestTimeout`, a `SamplingDuration` at least twice the `AttemptTimeout`, and so on). To add a handler of your own, chain on the builder the registration returns.

A [connection string](#the-connection-string) takes the same settings, as keys named after them: the last name of each setting (`MaxRetryAttempts`, `Delay`, `FailureRatio`, `PermitLimit`, and so on), except the two timeouts, which are `TotalRequestTimeout` and `AttemptTimeout` since `Timeout` is the client’s. They win over the keys of the section, and a setting turns the handler on unless the connection string also sets `Resilience`:

```text
Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;MaxRetryAttempts=5;AttemptTimeout=00:00:05
```

The code that reads the settings is written once for the project, `ChirographResilience.g.cs` next to the clients’ folders in `obj`, and shared by every client: only when the project references Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience.

## Service discovery

[Section titled “Service discovery”](#service-discovery)

Chirograph adds no service-discovery package either. When the project references [Microsoft.Extensions.ServiceDiscovery](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Extensions.ServiceDiscovery) (directly, or through another package or project such as an Aspire service-defaults project), the build sees it among the resolved references and writes the service-discovery code into the registration:

* it calls `AddServiceDiscovery()` on the client’s builder, after the authentication handler;
* it registers no provider: the application calls `AddServiceDiscovery()` on the services (an Aspire service-defaults project does), which adds the configuration provider (`Services:<name>`) and the pass-through provider, or registers its own after `AddServiceDiscoveryCore()`. Without any provider, [validation](#validation) fails at startup and says so, whatever the `BaseAddress`: the service-discovery handler resolves an `http` address too;
* `BaseAddress` may be a [service-discovery address](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/extensions/service-discovery), such as `https+http://rockets`;
* a client without a `BaseAddress` calls `https+http://<ClientName>`, so its endpoints come from `Services:<ClientName>`, or from the platform.

```json
{
    "Services": { "RocketsClient": { "https": ["https://10.0.0.5:8443/"] } }
}
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddServiceDiscovery();
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient();
```

Without the package, a client without a `BaseAddress` behaves as before, and a service-discovery address fails validation.

The authentication handler runs before the service-discovery handler, so the [host check](#which-hosts-get-the-credentials) compares the logical host, `rockets` in `https+http://rockets`, not the endpoint it resolves to.

## Configuring the client further

[Section titled “Configuring the client further”](#configuring-the-client-further)

The registration returns the `IHttpClientBuilder`, so everything `IHttpClientFactory` offers chains on it: handlers, resilience, lifetimes, and a base address of your own that wins over the configuration.

```csharp
builder.Services
    .AddRocketsClient()
    .AddHttpMessageHandler<BearerTokenHandler>()
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler();
```

Chirograph adds a handler itself only when `Authentication` asks for one, and resilience only when `Resilience` does. Handlers chained on the builder come after the authentication handler, so they see the credentials.

## Authentication

[Section titled “Authentication”](#authentication)

A client authenticates one of two ways. With `Authentication` set to a method, configuration gives the credentials and a generated handler sends them. With `None`, the default, the container gives the client its authentication.

### Configured authentication

[Section titled “Configured authentication”](#configured-authentication)

| `Authentication` | Keys                                                                                                       | Sends                                     |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `ApiKey`         | `ApiKey` (alias `Key`), and `ApiKeyHeader` (default `X-Api-Key`) or `ApiKeyQuery` (a query parameter name) | The key in the header, or in the query.   |
| `Bearer`         | `Token`, or `TokenProvider` in code                                                                        | `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.          |
| `Basic`          | `Username`, `Password`                                                                                     | `Authorization: Basic`, the two in UTF-8. |

`ClientCredentials` and `PrivateKeyJwt`, and the four Azure methods, are more methods, which the `OpenApiClient` item declares: see [Client credentials](#client-credentials), [Private key JWT](#private-key-jwt) and [Azure](#azure).

```json
{
    "ConnectionStrings": {
        "RocketsClient": "Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;Authentication=ApiKey;Key=abc123"
    }
}
```

The keys of a method other than the one chosen are an error, so a token left over from another setup can’t be sent by mistake. `TokenProvider` is asked for the token on each request that gets it, so a token that expires is fetched again by the provider, which caches it as it needs:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient(options =>
{
    options.Authentication = RocketsClientAuthentication.Bearer;
    options.TokenProvider = (services, cancellationToken) => services.GetRequiredService<ITokenSource>().GetTokenAsync(cancellationToken);
});
```

The handler is added to the client’s `HttpClient`, so Kiota and Refit go through the same pipeline. With `Authentication` set:

* **Kiota:** the adapter gets `AnonymousAuthenticationProvider`, not the container’s provider, so nothing sets the credentials twice.
* **Refitter:** the `RefitSettings` still come from the container, since they carry Refit’s serializers.
* `ConfigureRequestAdapter` and `ConfigureRefitSettings` still have [the last word](#the-last-word).

#### Which hosts get the credentials

[Section titled “Which hosts get the credentials”](#which-hosts-get-the-credentials)

The handler adds the credentials only to a request for the `BaseAddress` host, on its port, or for a host in `AllowedHosts`. An entry of `AllowedHosts` that is a host alone allows each of its ports; `host:port` allows that port only. A Kiota next-link to another host goes without them.

The handler also follows redirects in place of the primary handler (it turns the primary handler’s `AllowAutoRedirect` off, and follows as many as that allowed), so each hop is checked the same way: a redirect to another host goes without the credentials, whichever header or query parameter carries them.

With [service discovery](#service-discovery), the host is the logical one, and the endpoint it resolves to gets the credentials as well. A relative redirect resolves against the logical address, so it is resolved again and keeps the credentials. A redirect to another host still goes without them. A redirected request never carries the `Host` header of the first one.

A client with an `Authentication` needs a host to send the credentials to: a `BaseAddress`, or `AllowedHosts`. With service discovery, the default `https+http://<ClientName>` is one.

### Client credentials

[Section titled “Client credentials”](#client-credentials)

`ClientCredentials` gets an OAuth access token with the client-credentials grant and sends it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, through [Duende.AccessTokenManagement](https://docs.duendesoftware.com/accesstokenmanagement/) 4.x. The `OpenApiClient` item must declare it, because it needs that package (the declaration allows [`PrivateKeyJwt`](#private-key-jwt) too):

```xml
<OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" Authentication="ClientCredentials" />
```

The metadata adds a reference to `Duende.AccessTokenManagement` (the version of [`ChirographDuendeAccessTokenManagementVersion`](../../reference/properties/), unless the project references the package itself) and writes the code that uses it. Without it, there is neither, and configuration that names the method fails [validation](#validation) with a message that names the metadata to set.

| Key                     | Meaning                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TokenEndpoint`         | The token endpoint, an absolute `http` or `https` URI. Or:                                                           |
| `Authority`             | An absolute `https` URI whose discovery document (`/.well-known/openid-configuration`) gives the token endpoint.     |
| `ClientId`              | The client id. Required.                                                                                             |
| `ClientSecret`          | The client secret. Required. Keep it in user secrets or a vault, not in `appsettings.json`.                          |
| `Scope`                 | The scopes to ask for, space-separated. Optional.                                                                    |
| `Resource`              | The resource to ask for (RFC 8707). Optional.                                                                        |
| `ClientCredentialStyle` | `Header` (the default) sends the id and secret as HTTP Basic authentication; `Body` sends them in the token request. |

```json
{
    "ConnectionStrings": {
        "RocketsClient": "Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;Authentication=ClientCredentials;Authority=https://login.example.com/;ClientId=rockets-app;ClientSecret=…;Scope=rockets.read"
    }
}
```

The registration configures a Duende client-credentials client named after the client (`RocketsClient`) from the options, and the authentication handler sets its token, so the [host check](#which-hosts-get-the-credentials) applies to it as to the other methods. Duende caches the token and fetches a new one shortly before it expires (its `CacheLifetimeBuffer`, 60 seconds by default), so one token serves every request until then. A `refresh_token` in the response isn’t used: RFC 6749 §4.4.3 says the server shouldn’t send one.

With `Authority`, the discovery document is read on the first token request, not at startup, and cached (Duende.IdentityModel’s `DiscoveryCache`). Startup only checks that `Authority` is an absolute `https` URI, so a host starts without the network. The discovery document and the token request go through Duende’s back-channel `HttpClient` (`ClientCredentialsTokenManagementDefaults.BackChannelHttpClientName`): configure a proxy or a certificate for both there.

A token request that fails fails the call with an `HttpRequestException` that gives the server’s error, such as `invalid_client`.

#### The token cache

[Section titled “The token cache”](#the-token-cache)

Duende keeps tokens in a `HybridCache`. Chirograph registers none: Duende’s registration adds the default one, in memory. To keep them in [FusionCache](https://github.com/ZiggyCreatures/FusionCache) (2.x, which adapts itself to `HybridCache`), register it for the whole application:

```csharp
using ZiggyCreatures.Caching.Fusion;


builder.Services.AddFusionCache().AsHybridCache();
```

or for the tokens only, keyed with Duende’s `ServiceProviderKeys.ClientCredentialsTokenCache`:

```csharp
using Duende.AccessTokenManagement;
using ZiggyCreatures.Caching.Fusion;


builder.Services.AddFusionCache().AsKeyedHybridCache(ServiceProviderKeys.ClientCredentialsTokenCache);
```

The cache key is Duende’s: `<CacheKeyPrefix>::RocketsClient::<hashed scope>::<hashed resource>`. A distributed cache behind `HybridCache` shares the tokens across instances; encrypt them there if the cache is shared (see Duende’s [client credentials](https://docs.duendesoftware.com/accesstokenmanagement/advanced/client-credentials/) docs).

Duende doesn’t claim compatibility with native AOT: a native publish of a client that declares `ClientCredentials` warns about `Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid`’s default JSON serializer (its token cache), and works. A client that doesn’t declare it adds no package and no warning.

### Private key JWT

[Section titled “Private key JWT”](#private-key-jwt)

`PrivateKeyJwt` is `ClientCredentials` with a client assertion (`private_key_jwt`, RFC 7523) in place of the secret: the client proves who it is with a short-lived JWT signed by its certificate. The `ClientCredentials` declaration on the `OpenApiClient` item allows it. It takes the keys of `ClientCredentials` without `ClientSecret` and `ClientCredentialStyle`, plus a certificate, given with the [certificate keys](#client-certificate-mtls):

```json
{
    "Clients": {
        "RocketsClient": {
            "BaseAddress": "https://rockets.example.com/",
            "Authentication": "PrivateKeyJwt",
            "Authority": "https://login.example.com/",
            "ClientId": "rockets-app",
            "CertificatePath": "/run/secrets/rockets-signing.pfx",
            "CertificatePassword": "…",
            "Scope": "rockets.read"
        }
    }
}
```

The assertion has `iss` and `sub` set to `ClientId`, `aud` set to the token endpoint (the configured one, or the one the discovery document of `Authority` gives), a random `jti`, and `exp` five minutes ahead. It is signed through `Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens`, which Duende brings: RS256 with an RSA key, ES256, ES384 or ES512 with an EC key. The certificate is loaded for each assertion, and Duende asks for one only when it requests a token, so a renewed file is read on the next token request. Startup checks that a certificate is given, and that it loads with its private key. A `ClientSecret` alongside fails [validation](#validation).

A certificate has one role: the one `PrivateKeyJwt` signs with is not also presented for [mutual TLS](#client-certificate-mtls).

The assertion comes from an `IClientAssertionService`, registered keyed with the client’s name (`"RocketsClient"`). Duende asks the unkeyed `IClientAssertionService` for the assertion of each of its clients; the registration makes that one hand each client to the service keyed with its name, and any other to the service registered before it (Duende’s, which makes none, or the application’s). An `IClientAssertionService` of the application’s own registered after `AddRocketsClient()` would replace that one, so no assertion would be made: [validation](#validation) fails at startup and says to register it before, where it is kept for the other clients.

### Azure

[Section titled “Azure”](#azure)

The Azure methods get a Microsoft Entra ID token from an [Azure.Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/overview/azure/identity-readme) credential and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The `OpenApiClient` item declares them with `Azure`, which adds a reference to `Azure.Identity` (the version of [`ChirographAzureIdentityVersion`](../../reference/properties/), unless the project references the package itself) and writes the code that uses it:

```xml
<OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" Authentication="Azure" />
```

| `Authentication`        | Credential                                                 | Keys                                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `AzureDefault`          | `DefaultAzureCredential`                                   | `Scope`; optional `TenantId`, and `ClientId` (a user-assigned or workload identity) |
| `AzureManagedIdentity`  | `ManagedIdentityCredential`                                | `Scope`; optional `ClientId`, a user-assigned identity (system-assigned without)    |
| `AzureWorkloadIdentity` | `WorkloadIdentityCredential`                               | `Scope`; optional `TenantId` and `ClientId` (else the platform’s variables)         |
| `AzureServicePrincipal` | `ClientSecretCredential`, or `ClientCertificateCredential` | `Scope`, `TenantId`, `ClientId`, and `ClientSecret` or the certificate keys         |

`Scope` is the scopes to ask for, space-separated: `api://rockets/.default`, say. `TenantId` is a tenant id or a domain.

```json
{
    "ConnectionStrings": {
        "RocketsClient": "Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;Authentication=AzureManagedIdentity;Scope=api://rockets/.default"
    }
}
```

The client has one credential, made from the options the first time a token is asked for, and made again when the options are reloaded. The authentication handler asks it for a token on each request, so the [host check](#which-hosts-get-the-credentials) applies; the credential caches the token and gets a new one before it expires. Startup checks the keys only: it asks Azure for nothing. A credential that can’t get a token fails the call with Azure.Identity’s `AuthenticationFailedException` (or `CredentialUnavailableException`).

`AzureServicePrincipal` takes `ClientSecret` or a certificate, given with the [certificate keys](#client-certificate-mtls), not both. The certificate then signs the credential’s assertions, and is not also presented for mutual TLS.

A `TokenCredential` registered keyed with the client’s name is used instead of the one the method makes, for a credential Chirograph doesn’t make (`AzureCliCredential`, a `ChainedTokenCredential`) or a fake one in tests. The keys of the method are still checked, so pair it with `AzureDefault`, which needs only `Scope`:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<TokenCredential>("RocketsClient", new AzureCliCredential());
```

A native AOT publish of a client that declares `Azure` reports no trimming or AOT warnings.

### From the container

[Section titled “From the container”](#from-the-container)

With `Authentication` set to `None`, when the client is created, the registration takes its authentication from the container, under the key of the client’s name first:

* **Kiota:** an `IAuthenticationProvider` keyed `"RocketsClient"`, else an unkeyed one, else `AnonymousAuthenticationProvider`. An `IParseNodeFactory` and an `ISerializationWriterFactory` are looked up the same way, and Kiota’s defaults are used without one.
* **Refitter:** `RefitSettings` keyed `"RocketsClient"`, else unkeyed ones, else none (Refit’s defaults).

A provider keyed with another client’s name is not this client’s. The application registers them, so a client that a library generated gets its authentication from the application that uses it:

```csharp
// Kiota: a bearer token for RocketsClient only
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IAuthenticationProvider>(
    "RocketsClient",
    (services, _) => new BaseBearerTokenAuthenticationProvider(services.GetRequiredService<IAccessTokenProvider>()));


// Refitter: settings for IRocketsClient only
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton(
    "RocketsClient",
    (services, _) => new RefitSettings
    {
        AuthorizationHeaderValueGetter = (request, cancellationToken) =>
            services.GetRequiredService<ITokenSource>().GetTokenAsync(cancellationToken),
    });


builder.Services.AddRocketsClient();
```

Refit’s `AuthorizationHeaderValueGetter` fills an `Authorization` header that the operation declares (`[Headers("Authorization: Bearer")]`).

### The last word

[Section titled “The last word”](#the-last-word)

A delegate on the options decides what the client uses at last. It gets what the container gave; without it, the client uses that.

* **Kiota:** `ConfigureRequestAdapter`, given the adapter built over the client’s `HttpClient`. Return another adapter, say with an authentication provider of the library’s own.
* **Refitter:** `ConfigureRefitSettings`, given the settings from the container, or `null`. Return settings with a serializer or a handler set.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient(options =>
    options.ConfigureRefitSettings = (services, settings) => new RefitSettings { ContentSerializer = mySerializer });
```

## Client certificate (mTLS)

[Section titled “Client certificate (mTLS)”](#client-certificate-mtls)

A client can present a certificate to the server, for mutual TLS, whatever its `Authentication`, `None` included, unless [`PrivateKeyJwt`](#private-key-jwt) or [`AzureServicePrincipal`](#azure) signs with it. Give it as a file:

```json
{
    "Clients": {
        "RocketsClient": {
            "BaseAddress": "https://rockets.example.com/",
            "CertificatePath": "/run/secrets/rockets-client.pfx",
            "CertificatePassword": "…"
        }
    }
}
```

* A PKCS#12 file (`.pfx`, `.p12`), with its `CertificatePassword` if it has one.
* A PEM certificate with its key in `CertificateKeyPath`, the key encrypted with `CertificatePassword` or not.
* A PEM file that holds both the certificate and its key.

Or as a certificate in a store: `CertificateThumbprint`, in `CertificateStore` (`CurrentUser/My` unless it says otherwise). The keys work in a connection string too: `Endpoint=https://rockets.example.com/;CertificatePath=/run/secrets/rockets-client.pfx;CertificatePassword=…`.

The registration puts the certificate on the client’s primary handler (`ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler`), the `SocketsHttpHandler` or `HttpClientHandler` the factory made, not in a `DelegatingHandler`. It loads it again each time the handler is made, so a renewed file is picked up when the handlers rotate. The certificate is checked at startup, with the rest of the options: it must load, with its private key.

`ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler` with a handler of your own on the builder `AddRocketsClient()` returns (or a `RefitSettings` `HttpMessageHandlerFactory`) replaces the handler that carries the certificate. The overload that changes the handler, `ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler((handler, services) => …)`, keeps it.

## Without the registration

[Section titled “Without the registration”](#without-the-registration)

A generated client is an ordinary class or interface. Create one from an `HttpClient`, for example against a test server:

```csharp
var kiota = new RocketsClient(new HttpClientRequestAdapter(new AnonymousAuthenticationProvider(), httpClient: httpClient));   // or a provider of your own
var refit = RestService.For<IRocketsClient>(httpClient);
```

## With Dovetail

[Section titled “With Dovetail”](#with-dovetail)

A Dovetail joint is one more caller of the registration. See [With Dovetail](../../guides/with-dovetail/).

# Sources

> Where a client's OpenAPI document comes from, a file, a server project or a URL, and how Chirograph infers which from the item's Include.

A source is where a client’s document comes from. You never declare the kind: Chirograph reads it from the item’s `Include`.

| `Include`                                      | Source             | The document is                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| ends in `.csproj`, `.fsproj` or `.vbproj`      | **server project** | the one the project writes when it builds, through `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server`. |
| starts with `http://` or `https://` (any case) | **URL**            | downloaded on build, into the [document cache](../document-cache/).                              |
| anything else                                  | **file**           | that file, relative to the project.                                                              |

The rules are checked in that order, so a URL that ends in `.csproj` is still a URL.

## The document’s copy

[Section titled “The document’s copy”](#the-documents-copy)

Whatever the source, Chirograph copies the document into the client’s folder, `obj/<configuration>/<framework>/openapi/<ClientName>/`, and generates from the copy. The copy is only written when its content differs, which is what makes generation incremental: a server that writes the same document on every build, or a download that returns what the cache holds, regenerates nothing.

The copy keeps its source’s extension, which tells the generators JSON from YAML: `.yaml` and `.yml` for a file or URL that ends in them, and `.json` otherwise. A server project’s document is always JSON.

## Choosing a source

[Section titled “Choosing a source”](#choosing-a-source)

* **A file** when the document is owned elsewhere and you take its changes on purpose. The build never needs the network.
* **A server project** when the API is in the same repository. The client always matches the server you are building.
* **A URL** when the document is published by a running service. Commit its cache to build offline, and turn updating off to take its changes on purpose.

The guides cover each: [from a file](../../guides/from-a-file/), [from a server project](../../guides/from-a-server-project/) and [from a URL](../../guides/from-a-url/).

# Getting started

> Add the Chirograph SDK to a project, declare a client from an OpenAPI document, register it and call it.

This page takes a console application from nothing to a call through a generated client. The client comes from an OpenAPI file in the project. The [guides](#next-steps) cover the other sources.

You need the .NET SDK 10.0.100 or later: the generators run on .NET 10. The generated code is tested on `net10.0` and `net11.0`. Other target frameworks are not blocked, but they are untested.

## 1. Add the SDK

[Section titled “1. Add the SDK”](#1-add-the-sdk)

Chirograph is an MSBuild SDK. Add it next to your project’s own SDK:

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <Sdk Name="Chirograph" Version="1.0.0" />


  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

To pin the version once for a whole repository, put it in `global.json` and leave `Version` out of the project:

```json
{
    "msbuild-sdks": {
        "Chirograph": "1.0.0"
    }
}
```

```xml
<Sdk Name="Chirograph" />
```

Note

Chirograph has no release on nuget.org yet. Until the first beta ships, [pack it from a clone](#before-the-first-release) and use that version.

## 2. Declare a client

[Section titled “2. Declare a client”](#2-declare-a-client)

Put the API’s OpenAPI document in the project, for example `openapi/rockets.json`, and add an `OpenApiClient` item:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" Namespace="MyApp.Rockets" />
</ItemGroup>
```

* `Include` is the [source](../concepts/sources/): a file here. A project path or a URL works the same way.
* `Generator` is `Kiota` or `Refitter`. See [Generators](../concepts/generators/) to choose.
* `ClientName` names the client. Kiota’s client class is `RocketsClient`, Refitter’s interface would be `IRocketsClient`, and the registration is `AddRocketsClient()`.
* `Namespace` is optional. Without it, the code is in the project’s `RootNamespace`.

Build the project. The first build restores the generator, generates the client into `obj` and compiles it. Nothing is written into your project folder.

## 3. Register the client

[Section titled “3. Register the client”](#3-register-the-client)

The build also writes `AddRocketsClient()`, an extension on `IServiceCollection`:

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using MyApp.Rockets;


var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddRocketsClient();
using var host = builder.Build();


var rockets = host.Services.GetRequiredService<RocketsClient>();
var rocket = await rockets.Rockets[Guid.Parse("6f9619ff-8b86-d011-b42d-00cf4fc964ff")].GetAsync();
```

`Host.CreateApplicationBuilder` comes from `Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting`, which a console project references itself. A web project already has it.

## 4. Set the base address

[Section titled “4. Set the base address”](#4-set-the-base-address)

The registration reads the client’s base address from `Clients:<ClientName>:BaseAddress`, for example in `appsettings.json`:

```json
{
    "Clients": {
        "RocketsClient": {
            "BaseAddress": "https://rockets.example.com/"
        }
    }
}
```

Any configuration source works, so an environment variable `Clients__RocketsClient__BaseAddress` does too. Without a base address, a Kiota client uses the first server of its document. A Refit client needs one. The same section also takes a `Timeout`, default request headers and resilience, and the client can take all of them from a connection string, `ConnectionStrings:RocketsClient`: see [Configuration](../concepts/registration/#configuration).

## Before the first release

[Section titled “Before the first release”](#before-the-first-release)

Until Chirograph is on nuget.org, pack it from a clone into a local folder and add that folder as a package source.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/RocketSurgeonsGuild/Chirograph.git
cd Chirograph
mise install
dotnet pack src/Chirograph/Chirograph.csproj -o ~/chirograph-packages -p:Version=1.0.0-local
```

[mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/) installs the .NET SDK the repository builds with. Without it, use a .NET 11 SDK. Then, next to your solution, add a `nuget.config` with the folder (NuGet does not expand `~`, so give the full path):

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<configuration>
  <packageSources>
    <add key="chirograph-local" value="/absolute/path/to/chirograph-packages" />
  </packageSources>
</configuration>
```

Use `Version="1.0.0-local"` in the steps above. NuGet keeps the first package it sees for a version in its global packages folder, so when you pack again, either use a new version or delete `~/.nuget/packages/chirograph/1.0.0-local`.

## Next steps

[Section titled “Next steps”](#next-steps)

* [From a file](from-a-file/): a document kept in the project, JSON or YAML.
* [From a server project](from-a-server-project/): an ASP.NET Core project in the same build.
* [From a URL](from-a-url/): a document downloaded on build, with a cache you can commit.
* [With Dovetail](with-dovetail/): the client registered by a joint.
* [With Optionary](with-optionary/): `appsettings.json` IntelliSense and validation for each client’s section.
* Coming from somewhere else: [`OpenApiReference`](migrating-from-openapireference/) or [LaunchPad’s preview](migrating-from-launchpad/).

# From a file

> Generate a client from an OpenAPI document kept in the project, as JSON or YAML.

A file source is an OpenAPI document that lives with the code. It is the simplest source: the build needs no network once the packages are restored, and a change to the API shows up as a diff of the document.

## Declare the client

[Section titled “Declare the client”](#declare-the-client)

The `Include` is a path relative to the project. A `.json` file is read as JSON, and a `.yaml` or `.yml` file as YAML:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.yaml" Generator="Refitter" ClientName="RocketsClient" Namespace="MyApp.Rockets" />
</ItemGroup>
```

Anything that is not a project (`.csproj`, `.fsproj`, `.vbproj`) or a URL (`http://`, `https://`) is a file. A file that does not exist fails the build with [`CHIRO102`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro102).

## Configure the client

[Section titled “Configure the client”](#configure-the-client)

The project writes no code for the client. Its registration, `AddRocketsClient()`, reads the client’s options from `Clients:RocketsClient` or a connection string, takes a `configure` argument for code, and returns the `IHttpClientBuilder` for handlers of your own:

```csharp
builder.Services
    .AddRocketsClient(options => options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))
    .AddStandardResilienceHandler();
```

## Authenticate the client

[Section titled “Authenticate the client”](#authenticate-the-client)

Register the authentication keyed with the client’s name, then the client:

```csharp
// Kiota
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<IAuthenticationProvider>(
    "RocketsClient",
    (services, _) => new BaseBearerTokenAuthenticationProvider(services.GetRequiredService<IAccessTokenProvider>()));


// Refitter
builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton(
    "RocketsClient",
    (services, _) => new RefitSettings
    {
        AuthorizationHeaderValueGetter = (request, cancellationToken) =>
            services.GetRequiredService<ITokenSource>().GetTokenAsync(cancellationToken),
    });


builder.Services.AddRocketsClient();
```

See [Authentication](../../concepts/registration/#authentication) for the lookup, and the options’ delegates that have the last word.

## Several clients

[Section titled “Several clients”](#several-clients)

Give each client its own `ClientName`, and its own `Namespace` when they share a project, so their generated types don’t collide:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <OpenApiClient Include="openapi/rockets.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" Namespace="MyApp.Rockets" />
  <OpenApiClient Include="openapi/launches.json" Generator="Refitter" ClientName="LaunchesClient" Namespace="MyApp.Launches" />
</ItemGroup>
```

Two clients can share a document, for example to compare the generators. Each one gets its own copy of the document in its own folder in `obj`.

## Updating the document

[Section titled “Updating the document”](#updating-the-document)

Replace the file and build. Chirograph copies the document into `obj` only when its content changed, and the generator only runs again when that copy, or the client’s settings, changed. Saving the file with the same content regenerates nothing. See [How generation runs](../../concepts/how-generation-runs/).

## Passing options to the generator

[Section titled “Passing options to the generator”](#passing-options-to-the-generator)

`Options` is added to the generator’s command line: after `kiota generate …` for Kiota, and after the settings file for Refitter.

```xml
<OpenApiClient
  Include="openapi/rockets.json"
  Generator="Kiota"
  ClientName="RocketsClient"
  Options="--include-path /rockets/**"
/>
```

A change to `Options` generates the client again. Options that change where the output goes or what the client is called fight with the ones Chirograph passes; see [Generators](../../concepts/generators/) for what those are.

# From a server project

> Generate a client from the OpenAPI document an ASP.NET Core project in the same build writes, including servers with several target frameworks or several documents.

A server project is a project in the same build whose OpenAPI document `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server` writes when it builds. Pointing a client at it keeps the server and the client in step: change an endpoint, build, and the client changes with it.

## Make the server write its document

[Section titled “Make the server write its document”](#make-the-server-write-its-document)

The server references `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`, which builds the document, and `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server`, which runs the application at build time and writes every document it registers into the server’s `obj` folder:

```xml
<!-- Rockets.Api/Rockets.Api.csproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>


  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi" Version="10.0.15" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server" Version="10.0.15" PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

Rockets.Api/Program.cs

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();


var app = builder.Build();
app.MapOpenApi();
app.MapGet("/rockets/{id:guid}", (Guid id) => new Rocket(id, "Falcon")).WithName("GetRocket");
app.Run();


record Rocket(Guid Id, string SerialNumber);
```

The server does not need Chirograph. It can be a `.csproj`, `.fsproj` or `.vbproj`.

## Point the client at it

[Section titled “Point the client at it”](#point-the-client-at-it)

```xml
<!-- MyApp/MyApp.csproj -->
<ItemGroup>
  <OpenApiClient Include="../Rockets.Api/Rockets.Api.csproj" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" />
</ItemGroup>
```

Chirograph adds the server as a `ProjectReference` that is built before the client project, but whose assembly is not referenced (`ReferenceOutputAssembly="false"`). The client project gets no dependency on ASP.NET Core. Then it asks the server for the documents it wrote and copies the chosen one into the client’s folder in `obj`.

A document the server writes again unchanged, which it does on most builds, regenerates nothing.

## A server with several target frameworks

[Section titled “A server with several target frameworks”](#a-server-with-several-target-frameworks)

A server that targets, say, `net10.0` and `net11.0` is built as a whole, not for the target framework closest to the client’s. Its document comes from the server’s own build, so it doesn’t matter which frameworks the client targets.

## A server with several documents

[Section titled “A server with several documents”](#a-server-with-several-documents)

A server that registers more than one document writes each of them:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();       // "v1": Rockets.Api.json
builder.Services.AddOpenApi("v2");   // Rockets.Api_v2.json
```

Name the one the client is generated from with `DocumentName`:

```xml
<OpenApiClient Include="../Rockets.Api/Rockets.Api.csproj" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsV2Client" DocumentName="v2" />
```

`v1` is ASP.NET Core’s default document. Without `DocumentName`, a server has to write exactly one document; with several, or with a `DocumentName` that matches none, the build fails with [`CHIRO103`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro103), which lists the documents it found.

## Things to know

[Section titled “Things to know”](#things-to-know)

* The server runs at build time. Code in its startup that needs a database, secrets or the network can fail there; check `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server`’s documentation for how to tell a build-time run from a real one.
* The document is always JSON, as `Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server` writes it.
* The client project and the server have to be in the same build: a solution, or a `ProjectReference` chain from what you build.

# From a URL

> Generate a client from an OpenAPI document served over HTTP, keep it in a document cache you can commit, and build without the network.

A URL source downloads the document when the project builds. The last download is kept in a [document cache](../../concepts/document-cache/), so the build still works when the URL can’t be reached.

## Declare the client

[Section titled “Declare the client”](#declare-the-client)

```xml
<OpenApiClient Include="https://rockets.example.com/openapi/v1.json" Generator="Kiota" ClientName="RocketsClient" />
```

Any `Include` that starts with `http://` or `https://` is a URL. A URL that ends in `.yaml` or `.yml` is read as YAML, and anything else as JSON.

Every build downloads the document, and the client is generated again only when the download differs from the cache. When the download fails:

* with a cached document, the build goes on with it and warns with [`CHIRO104`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro104);
* without one, the build fails with [`CHIRO105`](../../reference/diagnostics/#chiro105).

## Commit the cache

[Section titled “Commit the cache”](#commit-the-cache)

By default, the cache is the copy of the document in `obj`, so a fresh clone or a clean CI agent has none. Name a file in the project with `DocumentCache` and commit it:

```xml
<OpenApiClient
  Include="https://rockets.example.com/openapi/v1.json"
  Generator="Kiota"
  ClientName="RocketsClient"
  DocumentCache="openapi/rockets.json"
/>
```

Now a CI agent without access to the URL builds from the committed document, with `CHIRO104`. When the API changes and the URL is reachable, the build overwrites the file, and the change shows up in your diff.

## Pin the document

[Section titled “Pin the document”](#pin-the-document)

Overwriting the cache on every build means a breaking change of the API reaches your client the next time anyone builds. To decide when that happens, stop updating the cache:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ChirographUpdateOpenApiDocumentCache>false</ChirographUpdateOpenApiDocumentCache>
</PropertyGroup>
```

With `false`, a client whose cache exists is generated from it without downloading anything. A client without a cache still downloads once to fill it. Then, to take the API’s changes on purpose:

```sh
dotnet build -p:ChirographUpdateOpenApiDocumentCache=true
```

and review the diff of the cache.

The `UpdateDocumentCache` metadata sets the same thing for one client.
